parsed_answer.content: The Optional class, introduced in Java 8 as part of the java.util package, is a container object which may or may not contain a non-null value. It was engineered specifically to address the 'billion-dollar mistake' of null references—the ubiquitous NullPointerException (NPE) that has plagued Java development since its inception. Before Optional, developers relied on defensive null checks scattered throughout business logic, leading to fragile codebases and 'code smell' where the intent of a method returning null was ambiguous: did it mean 'not found', 'error', or 'uninitialized'? Optional forces the API consumer to explicitly acknowledge the possibility of an absent value, shifting the burden of safety from runtime checks to compile-time design.

items: Optional is a final class designed as a value-based type; it is not intended for serialization or as a field in a class, as it adds unnecessary object overhead to the heap.
The monadic nature of Optional allows for method chaining, enabling developers to transform, filter, or provide default values without breaking the flow with nested if-else blocks.

Under the hood, Optional acts as a wrapper. While it introduces a slight memory footprint, the JVM's escape analysis can often optimize away the allocation if the Optional does not escape the scope of the method.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Insight: Never use Optional for method parameters or class fields. It was designed strictly as a return type for methods that might not return a result. Using it as a field is a serializable nightmare and adds unnecessary indirection. Furthermore, avoid calling .get() without checking .isPresent() first; it is functionally identical to a null check and defeats the entire purpose of the abstraction. Always prefer orElseGet() over orElse() when the default value requires a computation, as orElse() is evaluated eagerly regardless of whether the Optional is empty.

title: What is the Optional class? Why was it introduced?
